newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian cattle on feed still heading down.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian cattle on feed still heading down.

text.p: After a 23 percent fall in the number of cattle on feed in Australia in the six months to June, a further 13 percent fall was expected in the September quarter, the Australian Meat and Livestock Corp (AMLC) said in its August meat and livestock review.
This would bring the utilisation rate of feedlots to an all-time low of 36 percent, it said.
Cattle in feedlots fell by six percent to 434,000 head at the end of March from December, then fell a further 18 percent to 356,000 head in June.
The number is forecast to fall further to 308,224 head at the end of the September quarter, it said.

However, tightening of grain fed supplies in the United States, continued growth of the Japanese market and an increasing interest in forward contracts may contribute to Australian feedlot activity beginning to improve toward the end of the year, AMLC said.
The trading environment facing the Australian lot feeding industry had deteriorated substantially in the past 18 months, it said.

Although grain prices have begun to subside, they remain relatively high. Strong U.S. competition in the Japanese beef market had resulted in a 21 percent fall in Australian export prices to Japan, it said.
The appreciating Australian dollar had compounded the price fall for Australian exporters, it said.

While Japan remained the single largest market for Australian grain fed beef, the number of cattle destined for Japan at the end of June had declined to 235,000 head from 303,000 head in March and from 329,000 head in December.
An inability of Australian lot feeders to secure forward contracts had strongly influenced the placement of cattle on feed, it said.
"Even with an apparent bottoming in prices, forward orders appear to be required before lot feeders commit to placing cattle on feed," it said.
Trading activity in Japan had been subdued in recent weeks despite tight supplies of grain fed beef, it said.
The outbreak of E.coli pathogen had resulted in consumption falling for a wide range of food items, it said.
